item.title: Greenwood asks drivers to clear parade route by 1 p.m. on Dec. 4
item.description: Greenwood drivers have a 1 p.m. deadline to move cars off the Delta Band Festival and Christmas Parade route on Friday, December 4, 2026. The parade starts three hours later at 4 p.m. in front of City Hall, at Main and Church streets, according to the Greenwood-Leflore County Chamber of Commerce. The chamber asks drivers to avoid parking on Main Street if possible that day because entries will line up there. Its route map marks early Friday street closures with red dots and the parade route with green dots. A separate blue-dotted street remains open for travel between downtown and North Greenwood across Veterans Bridge. The chamber links the map from its parade page. For parade entries, the chamber identifies Washington and Main as the check-in intersection. The chamber says to approach by Walthall Street, then turn west on Washington. From its starting point near City Hall, the parade will turn north onto Howard Street. The chamber asks people on floats and in vehicles to keep candy and other objects aboard. Walkers are allowed to hand treats to spectators. The chamber lists 662-453-4152 for questions about the parade. Sources: https://www.greenwoodmschamber.com/annual-events/delta-band-festival-christmas-parade .

item.title: Leflore gained 30 retail jobs as Washington County lost 29 last December
item.description: Washington and Leflore counties finished December 2025 with a combined 3,481 retail jobs, just one more than a year earlier. That near tie conceals different changes in two Delta shopping markets. Washington County, home to Greenville, lost 29 retail jobs over the year. Leflore County, home to Greenwood, gained 30. Washington County counted 2,035 retail payroll jobs last December, down from 2,064 in December 2024. Leflore County went from 1,416 to 1,446. In the final quarter of 2025, Washington County had 183 retail workplaces and Leflore County had 136. Those establishment counts were down from 185 and 144, respectively, the year before. Average weekly retail pay rose in both counties. In Washington County, the fourth-quarter average rose from $558 to $604. In Leflore County it rose from $623 to $649. The averages cover all private retail jobs in each county, including those at chain stores and independent shops. Ahead of Small Business Saturday on Nov. 28, the figures supply a baseline for two counties, rather than an estimate for the whole Delta. They track jobs at local workplaces. They cannot say which merchants saw sales rise or how many people shopped in Greenville or Greenwood. Source records from the Bureau of Labor Statistics Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages. Washington County 2025q4 county payroll record: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2025/4/area/28151.csv . Washington County 2024q4 county payroll record: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2024/4/area/28151.csv . Leflore County 2025q4 county payroll record: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2025/4/area/28083.csv . Leflore County 2024q4 county payroll record: https://data.bls.gov/cew/data/api/2024/4/area/28083.csv . item.title: Washington County unemployment rises to 5.1% as Bolivar adds workers and reaches 4.4%
item.description: Unemployment rose in neighboring Washington and Bolivar counties in October, even as the counties’ employment totals moved in different directions. The Mississippi Department of Employment Security issued its preliminary October figures and revised September comparisons in its November 24 release. County figures count residents and are not seasonally adjusted. In Washington County, which includes Greenville, 784 residents in the labor force were unemployed in October, up from 713 in September. Employment fell from 14,832 to 14,711, a decline of 121. The labor force shrank by 50 to 15,495. The unemployment rate rose half a percentage point from 4.6% to 5.1%. Bolivar County, which includes Cleveland, added 43 employed residents, bringing the total to 10,104 from 10,061. Its labor force grew by 66, from 10,500 to 10,566. That left 462 unemployed residents, 23 more than September’s 439. Its unemployment rate rose from 4.2% to 4.4%. Mississippi’s comparable unadjusted unemployment rate rose from 3.3% in September to 3.6% in October. Washington County was 1.5 percentage points above the state figure, and Bolivar County was 0.8 percentage points above it. The county statistics describe the labor-force status of residents and do not count job openings. MDES monthly labor market report, October 2026: https://mdes.ms.gov/media/23357/labormarketdata.pdf . Separate county unemployment rate history: https://mdes.ms.gov/media/8735/urate.pdf .
